planting.note: Plant rooted runners or divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this montane Asian species prefers cooler root zones and more consistent moisture than the common European wild strawberries.

directions: Nilgiri strawberry is a wild species native to montane forest margins and grassy slopes from the Himalaya and the Nilgiri hills of southern India east through Yunnan and Taiwan, distinguished by densely silky-hairy, blue-green trifoliate leaves and white flowers. The small fruits ripen to a pale cream or blush-pink rather than red and are mild and only faintly sweet, so the plant is grown chiefly as an unusual textured groundcover and collector's curiosity rather than for its harvest. It spreads by runners more slowly than F. vesca, forming a tidy, low mat suited to woodland edges and rock garden margins, and the species has also been used in breeding programs as a source of resistance to red stele root rot. Give it partial shade and evenly moist, humus-rich soil, since it does not tolerate the hot, dry exposure that beach strawberry (F. chiloensis) shrugs off.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide and transplant small rosettes in spring into gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this high-altitude Himalayan species needs a scree-like root zone and resents soggy winter conditions.

directions: Dalton's strawberry is a diminutive alpine species collected from open meadows and rocky slopes at 3,000 to 4,500 meters across Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, and southern Tibet, far higher in elevation than any other strawberry in general cultivation. It forms a tight, slow-spreading tuft of small trifoliate leaves topped by white flowers with a conspicuous yellow-orange eye, followed by small, upright, orange-red fruits held above the foliage on short stalks. Because it comes from thin, fast-draining mountain scree, it performs best in a rock garden or trough planted in gritty, sharply drained soil and struggles in heavy or waterlogged ground. It is grown almost exclusively by alpine plant society members and specialist rock-garden collectors rather than for its sparse, mildly flavored fruit.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines
Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted runners or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; cloud strawberry is adapted to the cool, high-rainfall forest margins of the Himalayan foothills and prefers conditions similar to woodland-edge wood strawberry (F. vesca).

directions: Cloud strawberry is a Himalayan wild species, closely related to wood strawberry (F. vesca), native to temperate forest margins and open slopes from Pakistan east through Nepal, Bhutan, and into southwestern China at elevations of roughly 1,800 to 4,000 meters. Its white flowers and small, sweet red fruit are very similar in appearance and flavor to F. vesca, and it spreads by runners to form a loose, low groundcover in cultivation. The epithet nubicola, meaning 'cloud-dwelling,' refers to its native habitat in the cloud forests and misty slopes of the Himalayan foothills. It is grown mainly by collectors of wild strawberry species and in germplasm collections used for strawberry breeding research, and performs well in a cool, humus-rich woodland garden setting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bentham's cornel is markedly less cold-hardy than the deciduous dogwoods and needs a sheltered, mild-winter site.

directions: Bentham's cornel is an evergreen dogwood native to the Himalaya and southwestern China, unusual among cultivated Cornus species for keeping its leathery, gray-green leaves year-round rather than dropping them in fall. In early to midsummer it produces four large, pale creamy-yellow bracts around each small flower head, ageing to a soft pink, followed in autumn by pendulous, bumpy, strawberry-like red compound fruits that are edible but mealy and bland compared with Cornus kousa's fruit. It needs a mild winter climate and performs best in regions such as coastal California, the Pacific Northwest, and southwest England, where it is grown as a specimen or screening tree; it is considerably more tender to hard freezes than the deciduous dogwoods. Provide full sun to light shade and well-drained, fertile soil, and shelter young plants from drying winds until established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; large-leaf dogwood tolerates summer heat better than many dogwoods once its root system is established.

directions: Large-leaf dogwood is a vigorous East Asian species ranging from the Himalaya through China to Japan, grown for its unusually large, broad leaves up to eight inches long and for flowering several weeks later than most other dogwoods. In mid- to late summer it bears flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers without showy bracts, followed by small bluish-black fruits that attract birds, and the foliage turns a clear yellow in autumn. It makes a fast-growing shade tree or large specimen, valued by collectors for extending the dogwood bloom season well past the spring display of C. florida and C. kousa. Site it in fertile, moisture-retentive soil with some shelter from strong wind, since the large leaves can tatter in exposed locations.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting them where the mature trunk and limbs will be visible up close; the exfoliating bark is the primary ornamental feature and takes years to develop.

directions: Wilson's dogwood is a Chinese tree grown chiefly by collectors for its spectacular exfoliating bark, which flakes away in irregular patches of gray, green, brown, and orange to create a mottled, camouflage-like trunk pattern that has earned it the nickname 'ghost dogwood.' Small, flat clusters of creamy-white flowers appear in early summer followed by blue-black fruit relished by birds, but the plant is grown primarily as a winter specimen tree for its trunk rather than for its flowers or fruit. It is found in specialty arboreta and mail-order tree nurseries rather than mainstream garden centers, and performs best given full sun and good drainage to encourage the vigorous growth needed for bark character to develop. Allow it room to grow into a substantial small tree and avoid pruning that would remove the lower trunk where the patchwork bark is most visible.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or spring into moist, well-drained soil along streambanks or seasonal drainages in partial shade; brown dogwood tolerates periodic flooding but does poorly in constantly saturated soil.

directions: Brown dogwood is a California native shrub of streambanks, seasonal drainages, and moist foothill woodland from the Coast Ranges to the Sierra Nevada foothills, named for its smooth, hairless twigs and leaf undersides that distinguish it from the more common American dogwood (C. sericea). Flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring give way to pale bluish-white berries that are an important food source for native birds, and the plant forms an airy, multi-stemmed thicket along its native watercourses. It is used mainly in native plant gardens and riparian restoration plantings rather than as a formal landscape shrub, and performs best with the periodic winter wet and summer dry regime of its native Mediterranean climate. Plant it along a seasonal creek bed or in a lightly shaded native border with moisture-retentive but not waterlogged soil.
